rationale: Start with a broad gradient at an intermediate temperature to locate the elution window and identify critical pairs. The high final organic fraction reduces the risk of missing strongly retained compounds.

Test a substantial temperature change while holding the gradient fixed to reveal selectivity changes in the central cluster and late critical pair. The short initial elution window leaves ample room for later gradient shallowing.

Check the low-temperature endpoint to map temperature-driven selectivity before choosing a region to refine. Keeping the gradient unchanged makes the response of the crowded peak groups easier to assess.

Retain the favorable low-temperature selectivity and make the gradient shallower to improve the two unresolved pairs. The current last peak at 6.34 minutes provides room to gain resolution while targeting elution within 10 minutes.

Use a shallower gradient to strengthen separation of the remaining critical pair, while raising the initial organic fraction to offset the added retention time. Keep 25 C, which has provided the best selectivity.

Reduce the gradient slope from 0.035 to 0.025 organic fraction per minute to push the remaining critical pair above R = 1.5. Raising the starting organic fraction should help keep the last peak within 10 minutes.

The maximum CRF is already achieved; now test a shorter elution window by raising the starting organic fraction while preserving gradient slope and temperature. This may retain full resolution while bringing the last peak out earlier.
Return to the successful starting composition and shorten the gradient by one grid step. This tests whether the R = 1.61 margin can support faster elution without losing full resolution.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction separates the central pair again after its near-coelution at phi0 = 0.30. Keep the successful gradient slope and temperature, with injection 6 retained as the fully resolved fallback.

Raise the starting organic fraction another grid step while preserving the 0.025-per-minute gradient slope. This tests for a still shorter fully resolved method, retaining injection 9 as the faster maximum-score fallback.

Return to the fully resolved starting composition from injection 9 and shorten the gradient to accelerate late elution. This tests whether its resolution margins can sustain a steeper gradient without the selectivity loss seen at phi0 = 0.40.

Shorten the gradient further at the successful starting composition and temperature. Injection 11 has resolution margin in every pair, so this tests a faster method while retaining maximum-score fallbacks.

Shorten the gradient by one grid step to locate the full-resolution speed limit at this composition and temperature. If either critical pair falls below 1.5, injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by one grid step to test a different route to faster elution. Monitor both central and late critical pairs, since temperature can change selectivity as well as retention.

Explore a higher-temperature selectivity regime to see whether the central pair separates again beyond its convergence at 30 C. Injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback while this run tests substantially faster elution.

Test whether a steeper gradient at phi0 = 0.40 moves the central critical pair through its selectivity crossover and restores separation. This explores a faster region while retaining injection 12 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-score method.

Lower the starting organic fraction to counter the central-pair convergence seen at 30 C, while retaining a relatively steep gradient for speed. This tests whether composition adjustment can make modest heating useful; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Test whether heating at the higher starting organic fraction moves the central pair beyond its selectivity crossover into useful separation. This explores a faster elution window while preserving injection 12 as the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Slightly steepen the near-successful gradient from injection 17 to test whether the central pair gains separation while the neighboring pair retains adequate resolution. This targets a faster maximum-score method near a promising selectivity balance.

Test whether increasing the starting organic fraction beyond 0.40 restores central-pair separation after another elution-order crossover, keeping the previously successful 0.025-per-minute slope. Injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved fallback.

Narrow the successful injection-12 gradient window while preserving its initial composition, slope, and temperature. The gradient should still extend beyond the last peak, targeting the same full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient.

Test a slope of 0.055 per minute, between the fully resolved 0.050 and partially resolved 0.060 slopes. This refines the speed limit near the fastest maximum-score method without changing starting composition or temperature.

Shorten the programmed gradient to four minutes while preserving the fully resolved 0.050-per-minute slope. Its endpoint reaches the outlet at 4.65 minutes, after the demonstrated last peak at 4.14 minutes, so full resolution should be retained.

Test the minimum programmed gradient duration while preserving the successful initial slope, followed by a hold at 0.45 organic fraction. The central cluster should retain its separation, while this run checks whether the later peaks remain fully resolved and elute within 10 minutes.

Halve the slope used in injection 10 to test whether the higher starting organic fraction can support full resolution with a shallower gradient. The campaign has already achieved maximum CRF; injection 23 remains the preferred demonstrated method, with all peaks resolved by 4.14 minutes.
